e-5391.knowledge_point: Finding the Polar Equation of a Radial Line That Passes Through a Given Point
e-5391.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980294/assets/1e1362c20f9e20bb22d049d8b218d786a5254603ab4cc36d90b5866095a8897c.png)

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(6,-2\sqrt{3})$, find the polar equation of the ray.
e-5391.worked_solution:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-2\sqrt{3}}{6}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we find the angle in the fourth quadrant that has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}.
$$

e-5392.knowledge_point: Finding the Point of Intersection of a Circle and a Radial Line
e-5392.problem:
The polar curve $r=7$ and the ray $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980294/assets/728f7aad12a4f127cc002bc38c46fa87ba70d6ecd79ef311a0154014b649a0ce.png)
e-5392.worked_solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r, \theta) = \left(7, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =7\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{7}{2} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\  & =7\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{7\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(-\dfrac 72, -\dfrac{7\sqrt 3}2\right).$

decision.explanation: The point (4,5) lies in the first quadrant, and tan(θ) = y/x = 5/4. Therefore θ = arctan(5/4), option d.

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(4,5)$, find the polar equation of the ray.
after.worked_solution:
The angles that the ray makes with the positive $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the ray lies in the first quadrant, its polar equation is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the ray lies in the first quadrant, its polar equation is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980294/assets/03814c00b9e29f8a05507616ed08e3fe3daa484336e461012dc6c80799efc9e0.png)

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{6},-\sqrt{2})$, find the polar equation of the ray.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{6}}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the third quadrant. So, we find the angle in the third quadrant that has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}.
$$

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{6},-\sqrt{2})$, find the polar equation of the ray.
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{6}}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the third quadrant. So, we find the angle in the third quadrant that has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

after.worked_solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(8,\frac{5\pi }{6}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-4\sqrt{3} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =8\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-4\sqrt{3},4).$

The polar curve $r=8$ and the ray $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
content.worked_solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(8,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-4\sqrt{2} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =8\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-4\sqrt{2},4\sqrt{2}).$
